paras: The lynching of Ed Maxwell was the hanging of a prisoner, also called Ed Williams, by a crowd at the court house in Durand, Pepin County, Wisconsin, on Saturday afternoon, November 19, 1881. Accused with his brother Lon of killing the Coleman brothers the previous July, he was taken from the sheriff's officers at his preliminary examination and hanged from a tree in the court-house yard. The case drew national comment over a reported coroner's verdict that he had fallen down the court-house steps, a dispute over a reporter's account, and Southern retorts that lynching was not only Southern.

Maxwell and Lon, who used the name Williams, were wanted for shooting Milton and Charley Coleman, who had set out to capture them at Durand in July 1881. Arrested in Nebraska by Sheriff Killian, Maxwell reached Durand on Friday, November 18, in the custody of Sheriff Knight.

Crowds came into town on the morning of the 19th, and the hearing, put off by the district attorney until 2 p.m., filled the upstairs court room. Before Justices Dwyer and Huntington, Maxwell pleaded not guilty and waived examination. Accounts differ on what came next, but they agree he was taken from the officers and hanged from a tree in the court-house yard at about 2:15 p.m.

A visitor quoted by the Eau Claire Free Press said a 300-foot rope had been run from the bough of an oak about 150 feet away to the front portico. As Sheriff Knight led the shackled prisoner downstairs toward the jail, a pistol shot sounded inside, the noose dropped over his neck at the front door, and men at the tree ran with the rope and pulled him up. That witness and the Pioneer Press both put the crowd at about 500; the Pioneer Press said the widow, children and brother of one of the Colemans were present.

A St. Paul dispatch of November 22 said an inquest found that Maxwell "came to his death by falling from the court house steps and breaking his neck." The River Falls Journal later called this "purely an invention," saying no coroner's jury was impaneled. Sheriff Killian said the mob was unmasked and no effort was being made to bring the lynchers to justice, and no report of arrests or a trial was found.

After threats against the lynchers, the Durand Courier warned that there was "more rope here" for anyone attempting retaliation. In late December, fires destroyed the county buildings and about thirty stores at Durand, and were believed to be revenge for the lynching.

First reports ran in St. Paul and Chicago on November 20, where the Chicago Tribune headlined the Pioneer Press narrative "JUSTICE" and called Maxwell "The Red-Handed Desperado." Brief wire items ran from Sacramento to Vermont, and the inquest dispatch was reprinted in New York, Washington and Cheyenne.

Editors mocked the reported verdict, among them the St. Paul Globe, the Manitowoc Pilot and the Arizona Miner. The Pilot wrote that Maxwell "deserved death" but scorned lynchers who acted only because he was in irons, and later called the state's failure to punish them "a burning disgrace." The Chicago Tribune saw it as a symptom of distrust of the courts, while the Globe's telegram had reported local satisfaction.

Southern papers used the case as a retort: the Bolivar Bulletin wrote that "Mobs are not organized alone in the South," and the Marietta Journal quoted the New York Times on the brutality of the "Wisconsin mob." The Jackson Clarion said Northern papers were shocked that "a white desperado in Wisconsin" had been lynched, the only statement of Maxwell's race in the coverage.

The St. Paul Globe rejected the Pioneer Press account, saying its reporter had left Durand hours before the hanging. Where the Pioneer Press had Maxwell give a self-defense statement before men seized him in the court room, the Globe said he gave only his plea and was "nearly out of the building when seized." Sheriff Killian and the Eau Claire witness also place the seizure downstairs, though the Globe's own first telegram had him thrown out a window after repeating his claim in court.
Other details vary: one paper placed Durand in Minnesota, another said Maxwell "shot a sheriff," and the body was buried by town authorities in one dispatch and in the potter's field in another.
